D-GAM

D-GAM; develops an adaptable gamification conceptual model designed to increase user engagement and motivation into measurable, honest engagement.

ROLE
UX Researcher, Interaction Design
DURATION

THE PROBLEM

Imagine, there is a new retail store being proposed in your neighbourhood. You might have several questions and concerns. Being a resident you want to provide some insight, however, problem isnt access, the infrastructure for public participation exists, the problem is the lower motivational and sustained engagement in the infrastructure of public participation in built environment.

D-GAM framework was built to answer one question: can gamification enhance user engagement and motivation in participatory processes?

THE PROCESS

01. Problem Identification

What existing tools get wrong

A structured review of 37 civic engagement and gamification tools — narrowed to 17 targeting general public participation — revealed a consistent pattern. Tools that attract users rarely sustain them. When gamification existed at all, it was applied at the system level: the same points and badges for every project, regardless of context or stakeholder.

Four gaps identified in the same group

GAP 01

Fixed system-wide gamification

The same points and badges applied to every project, regardless of context, stakeholder type, or participation goal.

GAP 02

No mechanism for sustained engagement

Existing platforms attract users once but provide no reason to explore deeply, return, or contribute over multiple review stages.

GAP 03

Rewards motivate completion, not quality

Reward structures incentivise task completion as a checkbox rather than meaningful reflection on design alternatives.

GAP 04

AR novelty wears off quickly

Augmented reality tools improve spatial understanding on first use but do not sustain ongoing engagement without motivational scaffolding.

Research grounding

The framework was grounded in three theories. Self-Determination Theory defined what meaningful motivation requires — autonomy, competence, and relatedness. Operant conditioning explained reward timing. Flow theory explained how to keep task complexity matched to user capability.

02. Research Process

Four phase process

1
PHASE 01

Literature review & initial prototype

Established the foundations for D-GAM and built the first task-based prototype, grounded in Self-Determination Theory, operant conditioning, and flow theory.

2
PHASE 02

Evaluation & testing

Evaluated the first task-based prototype and tested it with a focus group of professionals.

3
PHASE 03

Formation of Flexible D-GAM framework

Based on the focus group findings, the task-based approach shifted to task-free, resulting in the adaptable gamification schema — four schemas mapped onto activities.

4
PHASE 04

Re-design and testing

Re-iterated the prototype implementing the four schemas, followed by a user study.

03. Design

From idea to wireframe to UI- V1

The first prototype followed a task-based approach. Users moved through a structured four-step review — select a project, explore the design in 3D and AR, review performance data, engage in discussion — earning points and rewards at each stage. This was the version taken into the focus group study.

Initial Focus Group Study

Based on the initial task based prototype; a focus group study was carried out, which included seven participants that were given an overview and interacted with the prototype and four themes emerged that fundamentally changed the direction of the framework. 

Results

DATA RECORDING

Sessions were audio-recorded and video recorded with consent and transcribed verbatim. Field notes captured non-verbal cues and moments of disagreement between participants.

THEME GENERATION

Transcripts were coded inductively using AI notebookKLM as , then grouped into candidate themes through affinity mapping and reviewed against the raw data for consistency.

Theme 1 — Rewards motivated engagement but lacked transparency

"I would like to know about the potential rewards in the beginning — it confuses me why there is a definite and an indefinite reward." — P1

Theme 2 — Task rigidity caused fatigue

"I have to add a comment under every section, which is a tiring process. Rather, I would prefer adding a combined comment at the end." — P3

Theme 3 — Intrinsic motivation mattered as much as extrinsic rewards

"Knowing my feedback will make a difference motivates me more than a material reward." — P5

Theme 4 — Users needed freedom to explore non-linearly

"I should not be forced to complete the tasks in order to earn rewards. I may switch to different tasks." — P1

The D-GAM framework — four schemas

D-GAM is built on four interrelated schemas. Each operates independently — meaning the reward logic, feedback model, project structure, or user tracking can each be modified without disrupting the others. This is what makes the framework adaptable across different project types and engagement goals.

4. PROJECT SCHEMA

Framework in action — four scenarios

To demonstrate adaptability, four scenarios were designed using the same four schemas — each with a different project context, stakeholder profile, and reward configuration.

Encourage deep exploration of form and AR views, with detailed qualitative feedback

Ensure users complete the full review including a final survey before reward is unlocked
Fixed only

New school — designers seek community dialogue and collective sentiment on proposals
Encourage discussion and reply chains between participants rather than individual review
Surprise only
S4
Full exploration for points accumulation
Any project where full exploration of all views is the primary participation goal
Increase task completion through direct redeemable rewards tied to exploration depth
Fixed only

Re-Designed Prototype

The redesigned prototype implemented the framework across two live project scenarios — a mixed-use building and a university café — each configured with different reward logic and navigation models. This video is demonstrating the first case scenario.

04. User Study

Participants

Ten participants were recruited through purposive sampling across design, technology, and academic backgrounds — none affiliated with the D-GAM project. Sessions ran remotely via Zoom, lasting 40–45 minutes each. Each participant interacted with two scenarios, completed a post-task semi-structured interview, and filled out a System Usability Scale survey.
